edits.before: Health misinformation datasets disagree about what misinformation is. FakeHealth labels mainstream health news by expert-rated reporting quality, whereas CoAID contrasts fact-checked COVID-19 claims with material from health agencies and health-information publishers. We compared model-standardized Fake/Real ratios of observed social-media posts, counting items never posted, between CoAID News and FakeHealth HealthStory, and evaluated leakage-controlled text classifiers within, across and beyond the two datasets. Fake items drew fewer observed posts than Real items in both datasets, but the ratio was 0.253 in CoAID and 0.840 in FakeHealth (ratio-of-ratios 0.301; 95% interval 0.154–0.645). The CoAID gap lay entirely in whether an item was posted at all and was concentrated among Fake items with no identifiable publisher, suggesting limited findability as much as limited spread. In two FakeNewsNet collections outside health, Fake items drew more observed posts in GossipCop (ratio 2.144) and PolitiFact's interval included parity, so neither the gap's size nor its direction carried across datasets. Text showed a parallel split: Fake and Real were highly separable within CoAID (macro F1 0.926) and modestly within FakeHealth (0.675), transfer was poor in both directions, and word–label associations were uncorrelated between datasets. Text length travelled better than words: shorter for Fake items in both datasets, it alone ranked transferred items and independent COVID rumors better than the word-based models. Period, labels, sources and collection differ together, so these are contrasts between dataset contexts, not pandemic effects. The distance between Fake and Real items, in language and in observed engagement, depends on how a dataset defines misinformation and where it finds it. The results are as much about data handling as about misinformation: engagement studies and detection benchmarks should report how labels, sources and collection were defined, check for source–label entanglement, shared-post dependence and simple length baselines, and test beyond a single dataset.

[Torabi Asr and Taboada (2018)](#ref-asr) found that classifiers trained on labels derived from source reputation generalized poorly to article-level veracity labels and performed unevenly across topics, although their predictions showed some correspondence with article veracity. [Murayama et al. Within-dataset scores are therefore informative about portability only when they are reported alongside transfer to other datasets, evaluated on the same target items.

Source and label are nearly the same variable (Cramér's V 0.971 against 0.352 in FakeHealth, in the text-modeling cohorts; [Supplementary Table S14](supplementary_material.md#table-s14-sourceclass-association-cramers-v)), text separates the classes almost perfectly (0.926), partly because Fake items are short excerpts and Real items long institutional articles and partly through words that separate them at any length, and Fake items draw about a quarter of the observed posts of Real ones (0.253). edits.before: Three explanations could produce this pattern, and they are not equally supported. The first is label construct and source ecology: the datasets define Fake differently and draw Fake and Real items from differently separated sources. This explanation accounts for every text result, provided that genre is counted as part of it: fact-checked claims are short statements in CoAID and COVID-Rumor, PolitiFact's titles behaved the same way, and length is the cue that carried between them. Between CoAID and FakeHealth, nothing beyond length carried: within length quintiles the transferred models ranked at ROC-AUC 0.50–0.52 ([Supplementary Table S19](supplementary_material.md#table-s19-document-length-as-a-shared-cue-scorelength-correlations-and-a-length-only-diagnostic-baseline)). For engagement, PolitiFact shows that the label construct alone is not enough: it shares CoAID's construct but not its engagement pattern, which shifts weight toward source ecology and toward what the Real class consists of. The second is collection and measurement. Both CoAID and FakeHealth gathered tweets by searching for item titles, and FakeHealth also searched by keywords and URLs, so search itself is not what differs. [Dai et al. (2020)](#ref-fakehealth), [Cui and Lee (2020)](#ref-coaid) What differs is how queries were formed, when crawls ran, and, in CoAID, how posts were pooled across repeated captures. These differences could widen the engagement gap but would not explain the text results. The hurdle components make this explanation more pressing, not less: the whole CoAID gap lies in whether an item has any observed post, which is exactly where differences in capture would show. PolitiFact, also collected by headline search, showed no Fake occurrence deficit, so headline search does not produce one by itself. The findability breakdown supports this explanation for the occurrence gap. Fact-checkers generally check claims that are already circulating, yet CoAID's Fake items had any observed post far less often when no publisher could be resolved (7.5%) than when one could (33.0%), and Real items first captured in CoAID's later releases were almost never posted either. Much of CoAID's zero-inflation therefore reflects what the collection could find and when it looked, and the occurrence gap is partly a measurement result. Resolved Fake items were still posted less often than resolved Real ones, so measurement does not account for the whole gap. The third is the COVID context itself: a crisis may shift attention toward official sources and change the language of both true and false claims. CoAID-trained models did transfer better to COVID rumors, but length alone matched that advantage, and it did the same for non-COVID PolitiFact titles. The ordering is therefore better explained by the shared short-claim genre of fact-checked items than by COVID topic or shared vocabulary, and it gives no support to a crisis effect on language. The first explanation, with source ecology weighted as heavily as the label, fits the full pattern most economically. The second cannot be excluded for engagement. edits.after:
Three explanations could produce this pattern, and the evidence for them differs. The first is label construct and source ecology: the datasets define Fake differently and draw Fake and Real items from differently separated sources. It is consistent with the text results if genre is counted as part of source ecology: fact-checked claims are short statements in CoAID and COVID-Rumor, PolitiFact's titles behaved the same way, and length is the cue that carried between them. Between CoAID and FakeHealth, nothing beyond length carried: within length quintiles the transferred models ranked at ROC-AUC 0.50–0.52 ([Supplementary Table S19](supplementary_material.md#table-s19-document-length-as-a-shared-cue-scorelength-correlations-and-a-length-only-diagnostic-baseline)). For engagement, the label construct alone does not determine the gap, because PolitiFact shares CoAID's construct but not its engagement pattern. PolitiFact also differs from CoAID in its Real class, topic, period and collection, and these data cannot separate those differences.

The second explanation is how posts were collected and counted. Both CoAID and FakeHealth gathered tweets by searching for item titles, and FakeHealth also searched by keywords and URLs ([Cui & Lee, 2020](#ref-coaid); [Dai et al., 2020](#ref-fakehealth)). The procedures also differ in how queries were formed, when crawls ran and, in CoAID, how posts were pooled across repeated captures. These differences bear on the engagement counts, not on the text results. The whole CoAID gap lies in whether an item has any observed post, which is where differences in capture would appear. PolitiFact, also collected by headline search, showed no Fake occurrence deficit, so headline search does not produce one by itself. The findability breakdown supports this explanation for part of the occurrence gap. CoAID's Fake items had any observed post far less often when no publisher could be resolved (7.5%) than when one could (33.0%), and Real items first captured in CoAID's later releases were almost never posted either. If fact-checked claims had generally circulated before being checked, these zeros reflect what the collection could find and when it looked. Resolved Fake items were still posted less often than resolved Real ones (33.0% against 57.6%), so measurement does not account for the whole gap.

The third explanation is the COVID context itself: a crisis may shift attention toward official sources and change the language of both true and false claims. CoAID-trained models did rank COVID rumors better, but length alone matched that advantage and did the same for non-COVID PolitiFact titles. The ordering therefore tracks the short-claim form of fact-checked items, and the text results offer no evidence of a crisis effect on language.

In sum, the first explanation is consistent with both branches. The second is supported for part of CoAID's occurrence gap but cannot explain the text results. The third cannot be assessed with these data.

edits.before: Fake health items drew fewer observed posts than real ones in both health datasets we studied, but how many fewer depended on the dataset: about a quarter as many in COVID-focused CoAID, where the shortfall came from Fake items rarely being posted at all, largely among items the collection could not trace to a publisher, and nearly as many in FakeHealth. Outside health, the gap was uncertain in PolitiFact and reversed in GossipCop. Text showed the same dependence on the dataset. CoAID's labels were easy to learn and hard to export, and FakeHealth's were harder to learn. Neither dataset's word cues carried over to the other; the one cue that did was that Fake items were shorter. The common thread is that the distance between misinformation and real news is set by how a dataset defines misinformation and where it finds it, and what a dataset counts as real matters as much as what it counts as fake. Fact-checked false claims, poorly reported health news and low-rated entertainment stories are different objects, with different distances from real news in language and in reach. Whether crisis periods themselves change that distance remains open. Answering it requires data that hold platform, labeling and observation windows fixed across crisis and non-crisis periods. Until then, any misinformation dataset should be read with care: engagement findings and detection scores should be reported alongside the definition of misinformation that produced them, the sources each class was drawn from, and the processing steps (item resolution, dependence and collection scope) that shaped the counts.
